title: After how many folds would a paper stack pass the Moon?
description: Starting from about ten metres after twenty folds, the video doubles the stack fold by fold, in metres and then in kilometres, until it is compared with the distance to the Moon.
teaching_notes: One idea: every fold doubles the stack, so a few more folds make it enormous, and each row of the table is twice the row above it. Watch for students who think growth stays slow because twenty folds give only about ten metres.

video_script.why: The child can double a height fold by fold, and now keeps doubling until the stack passes the Moon.
video_script.substitution: Keep doubling from about ten point four metres, change metres into kilometres when the numbers grow, and compare each new value with the distance to the Moon.
video_script.anchor: the book's thickness table for folds 21 to 45 on the board, with the Moon drawn at the top
video_script.payoff_line: The forty sixth fold passes the Moon

final_answer.value: Fold 45 is about 3.5 lakh km; the 46th fold passes the Moon at more than 7 lakh km
final_answer.spoken: fold forty five is about three point five lakh kilometres, and the forty sixth fold passes the Moon

never_show: any fold number other than 46 shown as the first to pass the Moon
maths_rules: a sheet is 0.001 cm thick; after n folds the thickness is 0.001 × 2ⁿ cm
fold 20: 0.001 × 1048576 = 1048.576 cm, which the book writes as about 10.4 m
folds 21 to 25: about 21 m, 42 m, 84 m, 168 m, 336 m
folds 31 to 35: about 21 km, 43 km, 86 km, 172 km, 344 km
folds 36 to 40: about 687 km, 1374 km, 2749 km, 5498 km, 10995 km
3.5 lakh km is 350000 km; 7 lakh km is 700000 km
video_script.design: One idea: keep doubling and compare with the Moon. The table and the Moon stay all video; the rows fill in groups of five; the check halves the last row.
